subject: chemistry_2
question_text: What happens when D-glucose is treated with the following reagents? i) HI ii) Bromine water iii) HNO₃

verification.note: Unit 13 (Biomolecules) is sourced from the chemistry half of "FAST TRACK IPE for Sr. Students", printed chapter 10 "BIOMOLECULES", book pp.99-104; the book prints this question on book p.101 as SAQ 2. The 1+1+1+1 mark split is a CLAIM, not the board's, until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. Neither the two-book union check nor a board back-test was possible for Chemistry-II: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is physics-only and first-year, and no second-year chemistry paper is in the corpus. BOOK NOTATION: the printed answer writes the reagent over the arrow as "Bro water" (a scan of "Br₂ water") and "HNO₃ (O)". Both are written out here. The printed answer gives the three reactions with no conclusions; the conclusions are added because they are the reason the question is asked, and the same book supplies them in its SAQ 12 table on book p.103.

steps.label: i) With HI
lines: i) With HI and red phosphorus, on long
heating, D-glucose is reduced to n-hexane.
Every oxygen atom is removed and the
carbon skeleton is left.
steps.why: HI with red phosphorus is a strong reducing agent that strips every oxygen atom out of the molecule, leaving only the carbon chain and hydrogen. Whatever is left must therefore be the carbon skeleton of glucose, which is why this reaction is the test for the shape of that skeleton.
common_mistakes: Writing the product as hexanol or hexanoic acid. All the oxygen is removed, so the product is the hydrocarbon n-hexane.
Writing the reaction as a short heating. It is prolonged heating that removes every oxygen atom; a brief reaction does not go all the way to n-hexane.
steps.memory_tip: HI takes every oxygen away and leaves the bare six-carbon chain.
steps.margin_note: The equation earns this mark faster than a sentence. Name the product n-hexane in words as well.

steps.label: ii) With bromine water
lines: ii) Bromine water is a mild oxidising agent.
It oxidises the –CHO group only, and gives
gluconic acid.
The –CH₂OH group at the other end is not
touched.
steps.why: A mild oxidising agent acts on only the most easily oxidised group, and the aldehyde is far easier to oxidise than a primary alcohol. So one end of the molecule changes and the other does not, which is what makes gluconic acid a monocarboxylic acid.
common_mistakes: Giving saccharic acid as the product. Bromine water is mild and gives gluconic acid; saccharic acid needs nitric acid.
Writing that both ends are oxidised. Only the –CHO end reacts with bromine water.
steps.memory_tip: Mild reagent, one end only: gluconic acid.
steps.margin_note: Name the product and say only the –CHO end changed. Both are needed here.

steps.label: iii) With HNO₃
lines: iii) Concentrated nitric acid is a strong
oxidising agent.
It oxidises both the –CHO group and the
terminal –CH₂OH group, giving saccharic
acid.
steps.why: A strong oxidising agent reaches the primary alcohol as well as the aldehyde, so both ends of the chain become carboxyl groups and the product is a dicarboxylic acid. Comparing this with the bromine water result is what shows there is a –CH₂OH group present.
common_mistakes: Writing gluconic acid for nitric acid. Gluconic acid is the mild oxidation product; nitric acid gives saccharic acid.
Writing that nitric acid breaks the carbon chain. The chain is unchanged; only the two ends are oxidised.
steps.memory_tip: Strong reagent, both ends: saccharic acid, an acid at each end.
steps.margin_note: Saccharic acid is also called glucaric acid. Either name is accepted; write the one the paper uses.

steps.label: What the three results show
lines: n-hexane shows the six carbon atoms lie in
an unbranched chain.
Gluconic acid shows a –CHO group is
present.
Saccharic acid shows a primary –CH₂OH group
is present as well.
steps.why: Each reaction is evidence for one feature of the open chain structure, and together they build it: a straight six-carbon chain with an aldehyde at one end and a primary alcohol at the other. Stating the three conclusions turns three reactions into an argument, which is what the examiner is marking.
common_mistakes: Stopping at the three equations. The fourth mark is for saying what each result proves.
Writing that n-hexane proves the presence of six –OH groups. It proves the six carbon atoms are in a straight chain.
steps.memory_tip: Three reagents, three features: chain, aldehyde, primary alcohol.
steps.margin_note: Three conclusions, one line each. This step is the difference between three marks and four.

insider_note: Three equations and three conclusions. Students routinely write the equations and stop, which caps the answer at three marks out of four.
